Design Patterns in C++
Chapter 0: Foundations: read, test, and choose a design pattern
Dr. Charles Dorner

1. Design patterns: make the next change safer
Problem and first design

SAY
Welcome to Design Patterns. Our job is to learn how to choose and defend an arrangement of code when a real requirement makes the current arrangement hard to change. A design pattern is a named solution structure for a recurring kind of problem. It is not a prize for using more classes. Throughout this course we will begin with working code, expose a specific limit, and then test a better arrangement. You will read C++ and diagrams together, predict what the program does, and explain what must remain true. Class 0 gives us the words and habits that make those later lessons useful.

DO
Open presenter notes for the spoken teaching script.
Ask learners to name one change that made an earlier program difficult to maintain.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.01: Teach the pattern, then test the design

------------------------------------------------------------

2. What counts as understanding a pattern?
Problem and first design

SAY
Knowing the name is the first step, not the final test. By the end of a chapter you should be able to describe the problem in ordinary words, identify each responsibility in code, and follow a request through the objects that take part. You should also explain a failure case and an alternative design. The strongest test is a changed requirement: can you place the change without breaking earlier behavior? A class diagram can look familiar while the code fails its contract. We will therefore treat names, diagrams, output, and tests as parts of one explanation, rather than four separate lists to memorize.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.01: Teach the pattern, then test the design

------------------------------------------------------------

3. Pattern, algorithm, and library are different things
Problem and first design

SAY
Imagine that a monitor must choose either an average or the highest reading. The steps for finding an average form an algorithm. The arrangement that lets the monitor use different algorithms through the same request may be Strategy. A standard library container, such as std::vector, is actual reusable code that stores the readings. These three things can appear in one program without meaning the same thing. A pattern does not give you a ready-made function to paste into every project. You must still choose data types, ownership rules, failure behavior, and tests that fit your program. That adaptation is where design judgment enters.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.04: Start with the pressure, then name the pattern

------------------------------------------------------------

4. Start with one requirement and one function
Problem and first design

SAY
Our first requirement is deliberately small. Two integer readings lie between zero and one thousand, and the program reports their integer mean. Integer division drops any fractional part, which is acceptable for this demonstration. The values two and eight therefore produce five. A function with two parameters is enough. Each parameter is a local value initialized from an argument at the call. The return statement gives the result back to main. We have no evidence yet that creating interfaces or rule objects would help. A clear precondition, a small calculation, and an exact output make this design easy to review.

DO
Predict the output before running the complete program.
Change the inputs to 3 and 8 and explain why the result becomes 5.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.04: Start with the pressure, then name the pattern

------------------------------------------------------------

5. A new requirement creates a design question
Problem and first design

SAY
Now users ask for the highest reading as well as the mean. That is a new requirement, not proof that the first function was badly written. For two stable choices, a small branch in one place can remain the best design. The pressure becomes stronger when several clients copy those branches, when rules change independently, or when a running program must replace its rule. Notice the order of our reasoning. We name the variation first: the estimate calculation. Then we ask where that variation currently spreads. Only after that do we compare a function parameter, an enum with a switch, and separate rule objects.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.04: Start with the pressure, then name the pattern

------------------------------------------------------------

6. A safe demonstration of duplicated decision logic
Problem and first design

SAY
This program has no dangling pointer and no mysterious crash. Its failure is easier to miss: two callers interpret the same request differently. The dashboard handles the highest rule, but the report still always computes the mean. For readings one and nine, the reviewed dashboard prints nine while the stale report prints five. Both calculations are valid C++, so compilation cannot identify the missing requirement. Keeping one shared function would already repair this small case. If independently replaceable rules become a lasting need, a Strategy boundary can keep both callers from owning their own copies of the rule-selection logic.

DO
Ask learners whether the compiler should reject this program.
Run it, then identify the earliest point at which the two callers assign different meaning to the request.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.04: Start with the pressure, then name the pattern

------------------------------------------------------------

7. Judge a boundary by the change it contains
Problem and first design

SAY
A boundary is the point where one part of a program meets another through a defined agreement. In our estimate example, a good boundary says what inputs the calculation accepts and what result it returns. The dashboard should not need to know every step of every calculation. However, a boundary does not always need a base class. One shared function could remove the duplicated logic today. A function parameter could let a caller supply a calculation tomorrow. A virtual interface becomes useful when named rule objects, stored choices, or lifetime management matter. We compare these costs against real changes, not against a rule that advanced syntax is always better.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.06: Three design habits that give patterns a purpose

------------------------------------------------------------

8. The creation family asks who builds the object
Problem and first design

SAY
The five creational patterns organize object creation. Factory Method lets a shared workflow ask a replaceable creation step for the object it needs. Abstract Factory keeps a family of related choices compatible. Builder makes a multi-step construction process clearer. Prototype creates a new object by copying an existing configuration with a stated copy policy. Singleton controls access to one instance, which also creates concerns about shared state and lifetime. These names do not describe five spellings of new. Each addresses a different pressure. During the chapters, we will ask what must be created, who decides its exact kind, and who owns the completed result.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.10: Choose a chapter by the problem; teach it through a change

------------------------------------------------------------

9. The structure family asks how parts fit together
Problem and first design

SAY
The seven structural patterns organize how parts connect. Adapter changes the form of a request or value so two sides can work together. Bridge separates two dimensions that must vary independently. Composite treats a tree of parts through a common operation. Decorator adds behavior around another object. Facade offers a simpler entrance to a subsystem. Flyweight shares suitable common data. Proxy stands in front of another object to control access. Some of these diagrams contain a field that refers to another object, but that shared shape does not make the patterns identical. We must ask what the connection is for and what the caller is promised.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.10: Choose a chapter by the problem; teach it through a change

------------------------------------------------------------

10. The behavior family asks how work is shared
Problem and first design

SAY
The ten behavioral patterns organize decisions and cooperation. Chain of Responsibility routes requests along possible handlers. Command turns a request into something the program can store or schedule. Iterator traverses a collection without exposing its storage details. Mediator coordinates participants. Memento records restorable state. Observer notifies interested parties. State delegates behavior that depends on the current state. Strategy replaces an algorithm. Template Method fixes a workflow while allowing selected steps to vary. Visitor places related operations over a type family. You do not need to memorize every mechanism now. Keep the problem verbs as retrieval cues, then replace each short description with a code trace as we study the chapter.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.10: Choose a chapter by the problem; teach it through a change

11. One chapter follows a chain of evidence
Problem and first design

SAY
We will use the same learning process while changing the problems. First, state a requirement and its limits. Next, make the simplest reasonable version and identify a specific new need it cannot handle well. Then introduce the feature or pattern that addresses that limit. Follow the actual code and diagrams, predict output, and run checks. Finally, break one promise deliberately, repair it, and compare a plausible alternative. This sequence prevents a common mistake: learning a pattern as a diagram detached from its reason to exist. When you review, practice retelling that chain in your own words before looking at the chapter answer.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.01: Teach the pattern, then test the design

------------------------------------------------------------

12. A type is a rule; an object is a particular instance
Problem and first design

SAY
A type tells the compiler what kind of value we are using and which operations are allowed. A class is one way to define a type that groups data and functions. An object is a particular instance of a type: two monitors can use the same class while holding different readings. A member belongs to the class declaration; a member function is often called a method. Object lifetime is the period in which that particular object exists, from completed construction until destruction begins. Pattern diagrams usually show types, but a running program contains objects. Keep that difference in mind when a diagram shows one rule box and execution creates several rule instances.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.05: The object words used by the patterns

------------------------------------------------------------

13. A value parameter and a reference do different jobs
Problem and first design

SAY
This example shows a mistake without causing unsafe memory access. add_to_copy receives a Tally value, so its change affects a separate parameter object. The tally in main remains five. add_to_original receives Tally followed by an ampersand, which declares a reference. The parameter is another name for the object in main, so adding three changes that object to eight. observe takes a const reference: it reads the same object while disallowing ordinary modification through that parameter. None of these calls transfers ownership. The original tally stays alive in main for all three calls, which makes the borrowed references valid.

DO
Predict both output lines before running.
Ask whether replacing a reference with a value is always a harmless optimization.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.08: Read the C++ used by the pattern roles

------------------------------------------------------------

14. An invariant is a rule the boundary must preserve
Problem and first design

SAY
An invariant is a rule that must remain true whenever a caller can observe the object at its public boundary. Suppose a monitor requires a usable estimate rule. Making its rule field private prevents ordinary outside code from directly clearing that field, but privacy alone is not enough. A public replace operation could still accept an empty owner and break the promise. A sound operation checks the proposed replacement before changing the current one. Encapsulation means placing related data and behavior behind a controlled boundary. The point is to make valid changes easy and invalid states hard to create, not merely to add the word private.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.05: The object words used by the patterns

------------------------------------------------------------

15. An interface includes promises, not just names
Problem and first design

SAY
An interface is the set of operations a caller may use together with the promises that give those operations meaning. An estimate function might require a nonempty list and guarantee a result within the range of its inputs. The nonempty rule is a precondition. The result guarantee is a postcondition. A permanently usable rule can be an object invariant. C++ function declarations describe types, but many of these value rules need written documentation and running checks. A function named estimate that silently returns Fahrenheit when callers expect Celsius can have the correct signature and still break the interface. Design begins with meaning before it becomes syntax.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.05: The object words used by the patterns

16. One request, two implementations
Problem and first design

SAY
Here the new requirement finally earns an interchangeable rule. Estimate declares a virtual operation named value. Mean and Highest supply concrete answers with the same input contract: integers from zero through one thousand. The owning pointer initially holds Mean, so the first call returns five for one and nine. Replacing it with Highest destroys the old owned rule and makes the next call return nine. Both calls use the same expression, rule followed by an arrow and value. Virtual dispatch selects the implementation associated with the actual object during execution. This small program demonstrates the mechanism that the Strategy chapter will examine in depth.

DO
Predict both calls and identify the actual object each time.
Trace what happens to the old Mean object at replacement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.08: Read the C++ used by the pattern roles

17. Read the diagram against the running estimate
Problem and first design

SAY
Read this picture from the actual code rather than guessing from its shape. The purple block is main and its local owning handle, not another invented class. Its filled-diamond connection says that rule owns the current concrete object through Estimate. The blue class blocks each point a hollow triangle toward their common base, which means public inheritance. Initially the owner contains Mean; assignment replaces it with Highest and releases the old object. The virtual value declaration explains why the unchanged call selects a different implementation. Added comments begin with Teaching and explain the excerpt. They are annotations, not extra UML relationships or executable steps.

DO
Point to each diagram excerpt in the preceding complete program.
Trace ownership at construction, replacement, and the end of main.
Ask learners to explain both arrow meanings before revealing the answer.

18. Read virtual, override, and const where they matter
Problem and first design

SAY
In the preceding program, virtual marks a member function whose final override can be selected through a base reference or pointer. The equals zero after the declaration makes the operation pure virtual: Estimate does not provide a usable concrete answer there. Mean and Highest use override so the compiler rejects a mismatch with the base virtual function. The const after the parameter list applies to the receiving object through that call. It does not prove that the function has no possible outside effects. The colon in class Mean followed by public Estimate declares public inheritance. Here it means that a Mean can be used through the Estimate contract.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.08: Read the C++ used by the pattern roles

------------------------------------------------------------

19. Access, ownership, and lifetime are separate facts
Problem and first design

SAY
Ownership means responsibility for ending a resource’s lifetime. A raw pointer can hold an address without saying who owns the object. A reference gives access to an existing object but does not normally keep it alive. In our rule demo, unique_ptr is an owning handle that releases the concrete rule when replaced or destroyed. The virtual destructor in Estimate lets deletion through the base pointer reach the derived object correctly. These are distinct questions: who can call the object, who controls its release, and how long will it remain alive? Many pattern bugs occur when a diagram explains calls but leaves ownership and lifetime unstated.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.08: Read the C++ used by the pattern roles

------------------------------------------------------------

20. Move transfers a resource only through a move operation
Problem and first design

SAY
The expression std::move is best read as permission to treat an object as a source for moving. The move constructor or move assignment that receives it performs the actual transfer. When a unique_ptr is moved successfully, the destination becomes the owner and the source becomes empty. That specific rule lets us trace ownership without inventing a second object. Other moved-from library objects have different guarantees, so do not assume that every moved-from value is empty. A design that keeps using the source must respect its documented state. Later patterns use moves to hand completed objects to their caller without copying exclusive owners.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.08: Read the C++ used by the pattern roles

------------------------------------------------------------

21. Read a range loop without guessing about punctuation
Problem and first design

SAY
When you see for followed by const auto ampersand child, a colon, and children, read it as: for each element in children, use a const reference named child. The colon belongs to the range-based for syntax. auto asks the compiler to infer the type; the ampersand avoids making an element copy; const limits modification through that reference. A const unique_ptr still permits changes to the pointed-to object unless the pointed-to type itself is const. Punctuation gets its meaning from context. A colon after a constructor’s parameter list instead begins member initialization, while a colon in a class declaration can introduce base classes.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.08: Read the C++ used by the pattern roles

------------------------------------------------------------

22. Separate what varies from what stays stable
Problem and first design

SAY
Cohesion asks whether the work inside one part belongs together. Coupling asks how strongly parts rely on each other. Neither word means that a program should contain isolated objects that never communicate. Our estimate callers must agree on inputs and results. The useful aim is a small, clear agreement that changes less often than its implementations. If report colors change for different reasons than temperature calculations, separating those responsibilities can reduce accidental edits. But guessing ten future variants may produce more complexity than the current task needs. Look for repeated edits, duplicated decisions, or a stated need to replace behavior before introducing an extension boundary.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.06: Three design habits that give patterns a purpose

------------------------------------------------------------

23. Composition keeps independent choices independent
Problem and first design

SAY
Suppose two report formats can each use three delivery methods. A subclass for every pair leads to six combinations, and adding a fourth delivery creates more combinations again. Composition connects a report to a delivery object so each choice can vary separately. In broad design advice, composition can include borrowing a collaborator; in a strict UML composition relationship, the whole also controls its parts’ lifetime. We must therefore inspect the actual ownership rule. Inheritance remains useful when a derived type keeps a base contract or varies a step in a stable workflow. The goal is to match relationships to requirements, not to ban one C++ feature.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.06: Three design habits that give patterns a purpose

------------------------------------------------------------

24. Single responsibility means one coherent source of change
Problem and first design

SAY
The Single Responsibility Principle asks us to keep a module responsible to one coherent source of change. A module might be a class or a source file. In our monitor, the alert rule answers whether a reading counts as an alert. A report formatter decides how accepted records appear on screen. A new workshop policy and a new color scheme come from different needs, so combining them can cause unrelated edits and tests to interfere. The principle does not mean every class should have exactly one function. A well-focused class may need several operations to protect the same data and fulfill the same responsibility.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.07: SOLID: five questions to ask about a design

------------------------------------------------------------

25. Open/closed protects a planned direction of change
Problem and first design

SAY
The Open/Closed Principle asks whether a known extension can be added without repeatedly editing the stable code that uses it. If the monitor calls an Estimate interface, adding another rule can leave its call site unchanged. Some construction or configuration code must still choose the new implementation, and that is acceptable. Closed does not mean no source file may ever change. It means a useful boundary protects one expected direction of change. Fixing a defect or changing the meaning of accepted input may still require editing that boundary. For a tiny fixed set of rules, a direct branch can be clearer than paying for an extension structure nobody needs.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.07: SOLID: five questions to ask about a design

------------------------------------------------------------

26. Substitution is a behavioral promise
Problem and first design

SAY
The Liskov Substitution Principle concerns what happens when a caller uses a derived object through a base contract. Suppose Estimate promises to accept every nonempty list of readings in a stated range. A derived implementation that secretly requires ten readings breaks that promise by strengthening the precondition. An implementation that returns a value outside the promised result range weakens the postcondition. Both errors can appear in code that compiles with override. The compiler checks signatures and language rules, while tests and review check units, values, side effects, and other behavioral promises. Run the same contract checks against every implementation, especially the smallest and boundary inputs.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.07: SOLID: five questions to ask about a design

------------------------------------------------------------

27. Interface segregation follows the caller’s real needs
Problem and first design

SAY
The Interface Segregation Principle asks whether callers depend on operations they do not need. An archive reader needs a load operation. If its only available interface also requires save, erase, and network setup, a read-only implementation may have to invent fake operations or throw surprising errors. Splitting reading from writing gives each caller a meaningful promise. One implementation can still support both capabilities. The aim is not the maximum number of tiny interfaces. Excessive splitting can hide which operations belong together. Start by naming the caller’s task, then group the operations needed to complete that task with a clear shared contract.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.07: SOLID: five questions to ask about a design

------------------------------------------------------------

28. Dependency inversion protects policy from detail
Problem and first design

SAY
The Dependency Inversion Principle concerns the direction of source dependencies. High-level policy says what the program must achieve. A low-level detail says how a device, file, or service carries it out. If alert policy directly depends on a particular file writer, file-format details can spread into the policy. An AlertSink contract can describe the delivery behavior policy needs. The policy depends on that contract, and a file sink or test sink implements it. The contract should express the policy’s need rather than expose every option of one file library. This makes a test implementation possible without making the domain decision about a physical file.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.07: SOLID: five questions to ask about a design

------------------------------------------------------------

29. Injection supplies a collaborator; inversion chooses the dependency
Problem and first design

SAY
Dependency injection means supplying a needed collaborator from outside instead of constructing it secretly inside the consumer. A constructor parameter is a common way to do this. However, receiving a concrete FileWriter by reference is still a dependency on FileWriter. It is injection, but it does not automatically create dependency inversion. To judge inversion, look at the declared types and what those types promise. A policy receiving an AlertSink can depend on the abstraction while a composition site chooses the actual file sink. That composition site is allowed to know the concrete types because selecting and connecting them is its job.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.07: SOLID: five questions to ask about a design

------------------------------------------------------------

30. Read class-diagram arrows as specific claims
Problem and first design

SAY
A UML class diagram describes types and relationships, not a sequence of calls. In these lessons a solid line with a hollow triangle points from a derived type toward its base. A dashed dependency arrow says that one part uses another. It does not imply ownership. A filled diamond sits at the whole end of a composition relationship. A hollow diamond represents aggregation, but by itself does not specify who deletes a C++ object. Some lesson legends explicitly annotate shared ownership; confirm that claim against the actual owning handles. Teaching connectors join explanatory notes to code and are labeled annotations so they cannot be mistaken for type relationships.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.09: Read diagrams as claims about code and lifetime

------------------------------------------------------------

31. Choose the diagram that answers the question
Problem and first design

SAY
One diagram cannot answer every question equally well. An activity diagram follows possible actions and decisions; its arrows mean execution flow. A sequence diagram puts participants across the page and calls in order down the page. A state diagram shows permitted changes between named states after events. An ownership view makes owners, borrowers, and release events visible. A state diagram does not prove that a program uses the State design pattern: an enum and checked functions can implement the same transition rules. Choose a diagram by the uncertainty you need to resolve, and then verify each arrow against the delivered source rather than treating the picture as evidence by itself.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.09: Read diagrams as claims about code and lifetime

------------------------------------------------------------

32. Trace data, control, ownership, and lifetime separately
Problem and first design

SAY
A single call can move control without moving ownership. In the estimate demo, main passes two integer values to the selected rule; the result comes back by value. Control enters the rule’s override and returns to main. The unique_ptr remains the owner throughout that call. Replacement is different: it changes which rule is owned and destroys the old one. Lifetime ends at destruction, not merely when an arrow in a call diagram returns. Following these four paths separately prevents the common mistake of assuming that a caller owns every object it uses or that a returned reference keeps its target alive.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.09: Read diagrams as claims about code and lifetime

------------------------------------------------------------

33. Compilation and execution establish different facts
Problem and first design

SAY
Compilation checks names, syntax, access rules, and many type relationships. It can reject an override whose signature does not match the base operation. Linking combines compiled pieces and may fail when a required definition is missing. Execution chooses branches for actual values, creates objects, calls functions, and destroys them. The stale report demo passes the build stages yet gives the wrong answer for the highest request. A virtual call’s required behavior is runtime selection of the final override, even when optimization can determine the target earlier. Keep the evidence precise: a successful build proves that this toolchain accepted the program, not that the program meets every requirement.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.09: Read diagrams as claims about code and lifetime

------------------------------------------------------------

34. Tests should challenge the promise, not just the happy path
Problem and first design

SAY
A test is most useful when it can catch a plausible incorrect implementation. An estimate test should distinguish the mean from the highest reading, rather than use two equal readings that both rules answer the same way. A replacement test should check both before and after the change. A rejection test should verify not only that an error appears, but also that any promised unchanged state really stays unchanged. Where ownership matters, observe a real destruction event with a valid lifetime-safe test. These checks provide evidence for the cases they cover. They do not prove every possible execution, every allocator failure, or every platform behavior.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.03: Build the demonstrations and read the diagrams

------------------------------------------------------------

35. Build one complete demo; know which version you ran
Problem and first design

SAY
Each runnable lecture demonstration is a complete source file, with its own main function and expected output. Build and run it separately rather than joining multiple files that each define main. The original chapter companions select C++17; these added lecture demos use an explicit C++20 mode and remain focused on the same mechanisms. Warnings are useful evidence about suspicious code. A failed build must not be followed blindly by an old executable with the same name. Compare the actual output, error stream, and exit code with the stated expectation. The larger companion checks include threading support where needed, such as the Singleton lesson.

36. Study Studio: turn watching into retrieval practice
Problem and first design

SAY
Use the chapter tools for different jobs. Start in Outline to identify the problem and the baseline. In Slides, pause before each run and say what you expect; open presenter notes for a fuller explanation. Use the UML views to verify relationships against code. Flashcards help retrieve terms and short decisions, while scenarios ask you to choose and explain a design. Coding Lab requires a working change that passes checks. In your notes, record the condition that must stay true and why your repair preserves it. Re-reading the same answer until it feels familiar is weaker evidence than producing an explanation before revealing the answer.

------------------------------------------------------------

37. Practice grows from a small edit to defended integration
Problem and first design

SAY
The exercise progression makes each new demand visible. A guided edit checks whether you can locate the right part. A trace checks whether you understand execution without relying on the compiler to explain it. A repair asks you to identify the earliest broken promise. A design comparison tests whether you can choose among reasonable alternatives. An extension then requires new behavior while preserving earlier checks. Finally, explain the decision in plain words: what changes, what stays stable, and what cost you accept. The capstone joins these skills around one contract. It does not ask you to insert every pattern into the same program.

DO
Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.

content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.10: Choose a chapter by the problem; teach it through a change

------------------------------------------------------------

38. Before Chapter 1: defend a simple decision
Problem and first design

SAY
Finish Class 0 by answering three questions without reading a definition. If a small program has two fixed output choices and no extension requirement, why might one switch be a good design? If users must add and replace calculations, what specific responsibility should become interchangeable? If a derived class compiles with override, what behavioral promises still need checking? These answers connect design restraint, variation, and correctness. Chapter 1 starts from a shared job whose record creation must vary. We will meet Factory Method only after that pressure is clear. Carry forward the central habit: explain the problem first, trace the mechanism, and judge the result against its promises.

DO
Ask learners to answer all three spoken questions before revealing the final answer.
Move to Chapter 1 and identify its varying creation step.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.10: Choose a chapter by the problem; teach it through a change

39. Teach the pattern, then test the design
Chapter reference

SAY
A student should finish a lesson able to identify the problem that needs a pattern, point to each role in code and UML, trace how those roles work together, and explain when the pattern is unnecessary. Recognizing a class diagram by its shape is not enough. The design must solve a stated problem.

Start each chapter with its concrete problem and the simplest reasonable approach. Let the limitation become visible before introducing the new arrangement. Then name the pattern and connect its roles to the program. The role table maps the standard role, the attached sample's name, and the name used in this chapter. This is the bridge between the supplied reading and the original teaching example.

Use the attached-example trace to revisit the provided code. Follow calls or ownership changes in their actual order. Then compare the new program. Ask which relationships stay the same and which language or application choices changed. The section on adaptations distinguishes the pattern's essential mechanism from optional features of one sample.

For a classroom demonstration, show the problem first, sketch the roles next, predict the call sequence, and run the complete example. Pause at each focused diagram page. Its code, line reading, and adjacent theory explain one important block. Finish by changing a requirement and asking whether the same design still fits. Each chapter supplies a specific teaching sequence and pattern questions.

Use the independent exercises in order: make a guided change, trace unfamiliar behavior, diagnose a defect, compare designs, extend while keeping earlier checks, and justify a decision. The implementation lab is a larger change with a runnable starting point and an explained solution. Pattern-check answers and exercise answers are kept in the separate answer section.

Read the short primer before the first pattern if objects, interfaces, ownership, or SOLID are unfamiliar. It defines the language needed for the pattern lessons. The course itself begins with Factory Method and continues through all 22 named patterns. The capstone then asks students to select and combine techniques rather than force every pattern into one program.

41. Build the demonstrations and read the diagrams

The -std=c++17 option selects the language version. The warning options ask the compiler to flag suspicious code, and -Werror makes those warnings stop the build. The -pthread option supports standard-library threading used by the Singleton lesson. The -o option names the executable. Python 3.9 or later runs the test driver without extra Python packages.

A class diagram shows types and their relationships. A hollow triangle points from a derived class to its base interface. A filled diamond sits at the exclusive owner. A hollow diamond labeled shared ownership marks shared ownership; the last strong owner controls release. A dashed dependency arrow means uses or borrows, not owns. Each diagram has a numbered relationship key.

42. Start with the pressure, then name the pattern
Chapter reference

SAY
This book teaches the patterns in the supplied reading and C++ examples. Its central question is "What change is hard, and which design makes it safer?" A design pattern is a named way to arrange program parts to solve a recurring problem. Its name helps a team discuss the problem, roles, and tradeoffs.

An algorithm is a set of steps that computes a result, such as finding the largest number. A pattern describes how responsibilities fit together, such as letting a caller choose among several algorithms. A library supplies usable code. A pattern supplies an idea that you must adapt. Two programs may use Strategy even though their class names, data, and algorithms differ.

Begin with a concrete requirement. A monitor must report one estimate from a list of readings. If the only rule is an average, one small function is enough. Now users need the highest reading too, and must switch rules during a run. A growing branch in the monitor mixes input checks with each rule. Strategy becomes useful when we want those rules to change independently. The extra objects have a cost, so two stable branches may still be the better choice.

Each chapter states a requirement, exposes the limit of a simple design, introduces the named pattern, traces and tests the solution, and judges an alternative. A pattern succeeds when it makes a real change easier while preserving required behavior. More classes or a familiar diagram do not prove better design.

DO
Ask students for a prediction before revealing the answer.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.04

------------------------------------------------------------

43. The object words used by the patterns
Chapter reference

SAY
A type tells C++ what kind of value something holds and which operations are allowed. A class defines a type that can hold data and provide functions. An object is a particular instance with its own identity and lifetime. Two monitor objects can use the same class while holding different rules. A member is a variable or function declared in a class; a member function is also called a method.

An interface is the set of operations a caller can use, together with their promises. It is more than a list of function names. For an estimate, the promise might require a nonempty list and return a value inside a stated range. An abstraction keeps the facts a caller needs and leaves out details it does not need. The monitor needs "estimate these readings," not the exact steps for finding an average.

Encapsulation puts related data and behavior behind a controlled boundary. Private members stop ordinary outside code from changing them directly. A monitor can reject a missing rule before replacing its current rule. Its invariant, a rule that must remain true at its public boundary, is that it has a usable rule. Merely making a field private does not protect it if a public operation still allows a bad value.

Inheritance defines one class in terms of a base class. Public inheritance says that a derived object can be used through the base type. This is a promise about behavior, not just a way to reuse lines. Polymorphism lets the same interface call reach different implementations. Through an Estimate reference, value() can run the Average or Highest implementation. C++ also supports other forms of polymorphism; these chapters mainly use virtual member functions.

Composition builds behavior by connecting objects. A monitor has a rule instead of inheriting every possible rule. In UML, strict composition also shows a strong whole-part lifetime relationship: the whole is responsible for its parts. In broader design advice, "favor composition" includes collaboration with borrowed objects too. Ownership means responsibility for an object or resource and its eventual release; access alone does not imply ownership.

A dependency means that changing one part can force another part to change. Passing a report type to a function creates a dependency on that type. An association is a lasting link between objects, such as a controller retaining access to a screen. Aggregation describes a whole-part grouping whose parts may live independently, such as a view grouping existing sensors. Its hollow diamond does not specify who deletes a C++ object. State ownership separately and check the actual code.

DO
Ask students for a prediction before revealing the answer.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.05

------------------------------------------------------------

44. Three design habits that give patterns a purpose
Chapter reference

SAY
Good design makes required behavior clear and likely changes manageable. Cohesion means keeping closely related work together. Coupling means how strongly one part relies on another. A useful design often raises cohesion and limits unnecessary coupling. There is no useful rule that all coupling must disappear: cooperating parts must agree on something. Aim for a small, stable agreement that a reader can explain and a test can check.

Encapsulate what varies. If new output styles keep changing a report calculation, separate formatting from calculation. The stable calculation can produce a result while a formatter chooses its presentation. First identify evidence of change: repeated edits, duplicated branches, or different user needs. Do not build a framework for a variation nobody needs. A function parameter may isolate the variation before a family of classes is worth its cost.

Program to an interface. A job that needs to store a result should ask for the storage behavior it needs, rather than reach into one particular file writer. The caller depends on a promise; implementations fulfill that promise. This permits a test implementation that keeps results in memory. It does not mean every class needs a separate interface. If there is one small, stable implementation, calling it directly can be clearer.

Favor composition over inheritance when separate choices must vary independently. With two report types and three delivery methods, making a subclass for every pair leads to six combinations. Connecting a report object to a delivery object keeps the choices separate. Inheritance still fits a true substitution relationship and a stable shared workflow. The question is which arrangement matches the change, not which language feature sounds more advanced.

DO
Ask students for a prediction before revealing the answer.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.06

------------------------------------------------------------

45. SOLID: five questions to ask about a design
Chapter reference

SAY
Single Responsibility Principle: keep a module responsible to one coherent source of change. A module is a part of a program that we can discuss as a unit, often a class or file. Suppose one class both decides which readings count as alerts and writes a color report. New alert policy and new report styling come from different needs. Separating those jobs lets each change without disturbing the other. This principle does not mean one function per class or one method per object.

Open/Closed Principle: allow a planned kind of extension without repeatedly editing the stable code that uses it. Suppose the monitor validates readings and then asks an Estimate for a result. Adding a Median implementation can preserve that monitor code. The program still needs code or configuration that selects Median. "Closed" does not mean never fixing a bug or never changing a requirement. It means protecting a useful boundary from a known direction of change. A small fixed set of choices may need no extension boundary.

Liskov Substitution Principle: a derived type must keep the promises callers rely on from its base type. If Estimate accepts every nonempty list of values from 0 through 1000, an implementation that secretly requires at least ten values breaks that promise. It has strengthened a precondition, a condition required before a call. Returning a value outside a promised range weakens a postcondition, a guarantee after the call. Derived types must also preserve the base invariants. Test every implementation against the same contract, including small and boundary inputs.

Liskov substitution concerns behavior as well as legal C++ syntax. A method can compile with override and still return the wrong units or reject a valid request. Replacing a base parameter type with a different type normally does not override the function in C++; matching the required signature matters. Do not confuse the broad idea of accepting more cases with permission to change a C++ override signature. The compiler checks part of the contract; tests and review check the rest.

Interface Segregation Principle: a caller should not have to depend on operations it does not use. Suppose a small archive reader needs only load(), but its interface also requires save(), erase(), and network setup. A read-only implementation then needs fake operations or surprising failures. Split the meaningful capabilities so a reader depends on reading. One implementation may support several capabilities. Do not split every method into its own interface: the goal is a useful contract for each caller, not the largest possible number of types.

Dependency Inversion Principle: high-level policy and low-level detail should depend on suitable abstractions; the abstraction should not depend on the detail. High-level policy is the rule that says what the program must achieve. Low-level detail is how a device, file, or service carries it out. Let an alert policy depend on an AlertSink promise. A file sink and a test sink implement that promise. Changing the file format then need not change the alert decision.

Dependency injection means supplying a needed collaborator from outside, often through a constructor. It can help implement dependency inversion, but the ideas are different. Passing a concrete file writer into a constructor is injection; policy can still depend directly on that writer. For inversion, inspect the types and their promises. SOLID principles help you ask questions. They are not five gates that force every small program to grow more classes.

DO
Ask students for a prediction before revealing the answer.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.07

46. Read the C++ used by the pattern roles
Chapter reference

SAY
The next excerpt becomes useful when an archive job must format records in different ways while keeping one workflow. Record names the common promise. TextRecord and BracketRecord provide choices in Chapter 1. A class body is inside braces, and the final semicolon ends the class declaration. public: marks members that callers may use. C++ has no separate interface keyword; an abstract class can express an interface.

Line by line: class Record begins the type. public: opens its public part. virtual ~Record() = default declares a virtual destructor and asks the compiler to supply its normal implementation. A destructor performs cleanup when an object is destroyed; the tilde marks its name. Virtual destruction makes deleting a derived record through the base pointer used by its owner safe. The format declaration returns a std::string, the standard library text type, and receives text as its input. The closing brace and semicolon finish the type.

In const std::string& text, the ampersand declares a reference: another name for an existing string, rather than a new string copy. const prevents changing that string through this reference. It does not promise that no other alias can change the same object. A value parameter would instead hold its own parameter object. The const after format(...) limits ordinary changes to the receiving object through that call. These two uses of const apply to different things.

virtual enables selection of an implementation through a base pointer or reference at run time. The = 0 marks a pure virtual function: this class leaves the operation to a derived implementation and cannot itself be instantiated. In a derived class, override asks the compiler to check that a function really overrides a base virtual function. final can prevent further derivation or overriding. Neither word proves the behavior is correct.

In Record* p, the star declares a pointer that holds an address and may be null. In *p, it follows the pointer to the object; a bad pointer makes that unsafe. p->format(text) calls a member through a pointer; a direct object uses a dot. A raw pointer does not state ownership. std::unique_ptr<Record> is an owning handle whose destructor releases its object. It permits one owner and cannot be copied. std::make_unique<TextRecord>() creates an object and returns its owner.

std::move(x) allows a move operation to be chosen; it does not itself move any object. Moving a unique_ptr into another owner transfers its object and leaves that particular source pointer empty. Do not assume all moved-from library objects are empty. The angle brackets in std::vector<int> or std::unique_ptr<Record> supply types to a library template, a reusable type recipe. You need to read these uses before you need to write templates.

In for (const auto& child : children), the colon means "take each element from children." auto asks the compiler to infer the element type; & borrows each element; const prevents changing that element through child. For a const unique_ptr this does not make the pointed-to object const. In a constructor, : member(value) instead starts member initialization. Context decides what the colon means. #include brings declarations from a header, std:: names the standard namespace, return supplies a result, and // starts a comment to the end of the line.

DO
Ask students for a prediction before revealing the answer.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.08

47. Read diagrams as claims about code and lifetime
Chapter reference

SAY
A UML class diagram shows types and their relationships. A solid line ending in a hollow triangle points from a derived class toward its base. A dashed line with an ordinary arrow shows a dependency. An association uses a solid line; an arrow, when present, shows navigable access. A filled diamond sits at the whole end of composition; a hollow diamond marks aggregation. A realization of an interface may use a dashed line with a hollow triangle. Read each page legend because line styles carry different meanings.

An activity diagram follows actions and decisions. Its arrows show possible execution flow, not inheritance. A sequence diagram places participants across the page and calls downward through time. A state diagram shows states and permitted transitions caused by events. An ownership view names owners, borrowed links, and the events that end lifetimes. Teaching links connect notes to code blocks; they are labeled annotations and are not UML relationships.

Compilation checks source syntax and many type rules, then produces code that the linker combines into a program. Missing definitions may fail at link time. Execution creates objects, selects branches, calls functions, and destroys objects. override errors can be caught during compilation. Choosing a valid but wrong strategy is an execution problem. Virtual calls preserve the required behavior of selecting the final override; a compiler may optimize how it achieves that behavior.

Trace four paths separately. Data moves as arguments and results. Control moves through calls and returns. Ownership moves only when the code transfers responsibility. Lifetime begins with successful object construction and ends with destruction. A borrowed reference does not keep an object alive. A retained pointer can outlive its target unless the design prevents that. In each chapter, ask who creates each object, who may call it, who releases it, and which tests cover those promises.

DO
Ask students for a prediction before revealing the answer.

SOURCE
content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.09

48. Choose a chapter by the problem; teach it through a change
Chapter reference

SAY
The catalog follows the supplied material: five creational patterns, seven structural patterns, and ten behavioral patterns. Creational patterns organize object creation. Structural patterns organize how parts fit together. Behavioral patterns organize decisions and cooperation. The table is a starting point, not an automatic selector. Several patterns can fit one program; compare their intent before comparing their box shapes.

For a class session, spend ten minutes on the simple design, ten on a new need that breaks it, fifteen tracing the solution and diagram, and fifteen making and testing one change. Use ten minutes to compare alternatives. Adjust the time to the class; require learners to predict behavior before running code.

Follow the exercises: guided change, code trace, bug repair, design choice, tested extension, and plain-English justification. In the capstone, name each pattern role in the source and state one invariant per boundary. Correct output is necessary; explain why the design stays correct under change.

49. Application case 1
Chapter reference

SAY
A reviewer says a class compiles with override, so it must satisfy the base contract. What should the team conclude?

Open Scenarios to select an answer and compare the reasoning for all four choices.

Ownership is automatically shared.. override says nothing about who owns an object.

Virtual calls always create new objects.. Dispatch selects a function implementation; it does not imply allocation.

Every valid input must now be accepted.. The compiler does not prove all preconditions are preserved.

The signature matches, but behavior still needs review and tests.. override checks an overriding relationship, not every input, result, or lifetime promise.

50. Application case 2
Chapter reference

SAY
A small program has two fixed output choices and one switch. No extension requirement exists. What is the strongest design decision?

Open Scenarios to select an answer and compare the reasoning for all four choices.

Add a hierarchy for each choice immediately.. More types alone do not solve an observed limitation.

Use every creational pattern to future-proof it.. Unneeded extension points add maintenance work.

Remove the tests because the program is small.. A simple implementation still needs correct behavior.

Keep the direct design while testing its contract.. A pattern earns its cost by addressing a real source of variation.
